pathway.title: Web Development
pathway.description: A progressive pathway for planning, building, testing, securing and operating modern websites and web applications.

course.title: Web Development — Intermediate
course.minimum_runtime_version: Modern evergreen browser and Node.js 20+ for tooling
course.dependencies: Standards-based browser APIs; optional tooling must be documented and version-pinned.
course.short_description: Develop multi-page, data-driven front-end applications with modern JavaScript, APIs, state, routing and testing.
course.prerequisites: Completion of Web Development — Beginner or equivalent ability with semantic HTML, responsive CSS, JavaScript functions, arrays, objects and DOM events.
learning_outcomes: Build multi-page interfaces with reusable components and maintainable CSS.
Fetch and validate remote data while handling loading, empty and error states.
Manage client-side state, forms, navigation and browser persistence.
Test responsive, accessible applications and prepare reliable builds.

topics.title: Component thinking and separation of concerns
topics.description: A guided lesson about component thinking and separation of concerns with examples and practical application.

lesson.title: Component thinking and separation of concerns
objectives: Explain the core ideas behind component thinking and separation of concerns.
Apply component thinking and separation of concerns in a small, testable web-development task.
Evaluate accessibility, security or maintainability implications relevant to component thinking and separation of concerns.

blocks.title: Concepts and engineering context
blocks.body:
An intermediate web application coordinates interface components, application state, navigation and remote data. The key engineering challenge is to make these parts cooperate without allowing every component to own every concern. Separate domain rules from rendering, keep network access behind a small service boundary, and make state transitions explicit. A page that requests data needs at least loading, success, empty and failure states; otherwise users may see a blank screen or stale information when the network is slow. Treat all remote data as untrusted: validate its shape before using it, encode or safely render user-provided text, and distinguish HTTP failures from network failures. Browser history and URL parameters are part of the user experience because they support refresh, sharing and back/forward navigation. Reusable components should expose clear inputs and events rather than reach into unrelated global state. Automated tests should cover domain logic and important interface behavior, while manual checks verify keyboard operation, responsive layout and assistive-technology usability. A production build should use explicit environment configuration and must never embed private server credentials in browser-delivered code.

In this lesson, focus specifically on component thinking and separation of concerns. Start by stating the user need and the expected behavior. Identify the browser or server responsibility involved, then select the smallest standards-based tool that solves the problem. Work through one normal case and at least one boundary case. Inspect the result in developer tools, explain why the implementation behaves as it does, and record assumptions that would need verification in a real deployment. Avoid copying a framework pattern without understanding the browser or HTTP behavior underneath it.

blocks.explanation: This small JavaScript example models data and transforms it into a readable summary. It runs in Node.js and demonstrates the language behavior used in browser scripts; the surrounding lesson explains how the same idea fits into web architecture.

objectives: Explain the core ideas behind persistence, caching and data validation.
Apply persistence, caching and data validation in a small, testable web-development task.
Evaluate accessibility, security or maintainability implications relevant to persistence, caching and data validation.

blocks.title: Concepts and engineering context
blocks.body:
An intermediate web application coordinates interface components, application state, navigation and remote data. The key engineering challenge is to make these parts cooperate without allowing every component to own every concern. Separate domain rules from rendering, keep network access behind a small service boundary, and make state transitions explicit. A page that requests data needs at least loading, success, empty and failure states; otherwise users may see a blank screen or stale information when the network is slow. Treat all remote data as untrusted: validate its shape before using it, encode or safely render user-provided text, and distinguish HTTP failures from network failures. Browser history and URL parameters are part of the user experience because they support refresh, sharing and back/forward navigation. Reusable components should expose clear inputs and events rather than reach into unrelated global state. Automated tests should cover domain logic and important interface behavior, while manual checks verify keyboard operation, responsive layout and assistive-technology usability. A production build should use explicit environment configuration and must never embed private server credentials in browser-delivered code.

In this lesson, focus specifically on persistence, caching and data validation. Start by stating the user need and the expected behavior. Identify the browser or server responsibility involved, then select the smallest standards-based tool that solves the problem. Work through one normal case and at least one boundary case. Inspect the result in developer tools, explain why the implementation behaves as it does, and record assumptions that would need verification in a real deployment. Avoid copying a framework pattern without understanding the browser or HTTP behavior underneath it.

practical_project.title: Web Development — Intermediate Capstone
practical_project.purpose: Design and build a data-driven multi-page front-end application that demonstrates the course outcomes.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional data and test accounts only; do not connect to Marian production systems or real learner records.
Do not put credentials, API secrets or private keys in browser code.
A learning prototype is not a security certification or production approval.
requirements: Write a short user and feature brief with acceptance criteria.
Use semantic HTML, responsive CSS and a clear component or page structure.
Implement the required interactions and validate user input.
Handle empty, loading, success and error states where data is asynchronous.
Include keyboard and accessibility checks appropriate to the interface.
Add automated tests for important behavior and document setup and limitations.
suggested_steps: Define users, scope, acceptance criteria and a simple architecture diagram.
Build the semantic structure and responsive visual system.
Implement behavior and data boundaries in small increments.
Test normal, boundary, accessibility and failure cases.
Review performance, security and maintainability appropriate to the level.
Document setup, screenshots, decisions and known limitations.
success_checks: The application satisfies its stated acceptance criteria.
The interface works at mobile and desktop widths.
Core tasks are possible using a keyboard.
Important normal and failure cases are tested.
The README explains setup, architecture and limitations.

rubric.look_for: Clear scope, coherent structure and justified design decisions.
Correct behavior, readable code and maintainable organization.
Semantic structure, keyboard use, contrast and adaptable layout.
Relevant automated and manual tests, including boundary cases.
Reproducible setup, diagrams, trade-offs and honest limitations.
